name: 2. Requirements analysis
description: Functional and non-functional requirements, roles, compliance, integrations.

groups.gg: requirements example from the company projects

cards.subject: A business requirement
says: states the goal the organisation wants to reach by funding the project
is written in terms of outcomes for the business rather than features
is the reason the other requirements exist
cards.use: need to explain why the project is worth doing
not: lists the screens and fields of the user interface

cards.subject: A user requirement
says: describes what a group of users needs to be able to do
is usually phrased from the point of view of a role
sits between the business goal and the detailed system behaviour
cards.use: collect what a role needs before any design exists
not: describes the database tables the system must contain

cards.subject: A functional requirement
says: states a behaviour or function the system must perform
can be demonstrated by giving an input and observing an output
describes what the system does rather than how well it does it
cards.use: need to say what the system must do in response to an action
not: states how fast the system must respond under load

cards.subject: A non-functional requirement
says: states a quality the system must have, such as speed or availability
applies across many features rather than to one feature
shapes architecture choices and is costly to retrofit
cards.use: need to state how well the system must work
not: describes one function that a single user can trigger

cards.subject: A constraint
says: limits the solutions the team may choose
comes from outside the team, for example the platform, budget or a regulation
is not negotiable in the way a feature wish is
cards.use: learn that production runs an older runtime so newer APIs are off limits
not: is a feature the team picks to delight users

cards.subject: A business rule
says: is a policy or condition of the organisation that the system must enforce
exists independently of any software
is often expressed as if-then statements about data or decisions
cards.use: hear that a refund over a set amount needs a manager's approval
not: is a prediction about the future that nobody has checked

cards.subject: An assumption
says: is something believed true but not yet confirmed
becomes a risk if it turns out to be false
should be written down with an owner who will confirm it
cards.use: find that the plan depends on a third party API staying free
not: is a rule the system is forced to follow by law

cards.subject: A transition requirement
says: covers what is needed to move from the old way of working to the new system
includes data migration, training and cut-over steps
stops being needed once the system is fully live
cards.use: must plan how existing records reach the new system on launch day
not: describes a quality such as availability that lasts for the life of the system

cards.subject: A derived requirement
says: follows from another requirement rather than being asked for directly
must keep a link back to the requirement it came from
appears when a high-level need is broken down during analysis
cards.use: split one high-level need into several lower-level ones
not: is invented by the developer with no source

cards.subject: A user story
says: is a short sentence naming a role, an action and a benefit
is a prompt for a conversation rather than a full specification
is normally written in the form as a role, I want an action, so that a benefit
cards.use: need a lightweight way to capture a need from a user's view
not: is a complete contract that replaces all discussion

cards.subject: An epic
says: is a large story too big to finish in one iteration
is split into smaller stories before it is built
groups related stories under one broad goal
cards.use: find a story is too large to deliver in a single sprint
not: is a single check used to decide if a story is done

cards.subject: Acceptance criteria
says: are the checks that decide whether a story is done
are specific enough that two people would reach the same pass or fail result
are agreed before development starts
cards.use: need an objective way to decide if work meets the need
not: are the estimate of how many hours a story will take

cards.subject: The definition of done
says: is a shared checklist that applies to every story
covers things such as review, testing and documentation
is the same for all stories whereas acceptance criteria differ per story
cards.use: need one quality bar that every item must clear
not: is written fresh for each individual story

cards.subject: The Given-When-Then format
says: writes a criterion as a starting state, an action and an expected result
comes from behaviour-driven development
turns a rule into an example that can be automated
cards.use: want criteria that read like a runnable scenario
not: is a prioritisation scheme with three levels

cards.subject: A rule-based criterion list
says: states acceptance criteria as a bullet list of rules
suits constraints that hold in every case
is shorter than writing a scenario for each rule
cards.use: need to record simple rules such as a pass mark of 80 percent
not: describes a path through a dialogue between user and system step by step

cards.subject: The INVEST checklist
says: tests whether a story is Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable
is used to review the quality of stories before a sprint
flags a story that is too big or cannot be tested
cards.use: want a quick test of whether a story is ready
not: is a template for writing use case steps

cards.subject: The definition of ready
says: lists what a story needs before the team will take it into a sprint
often includes clear criteria and a known owner for open questions
protects the team from starting work on unclear items
cards.use: keep vague items out of the sprint
not: lists what must be true before a release goes to production

cards.subject: A story map
says: arranges stories along the steps of a user's journey
shows the backbone of activities with details underneath
helps cut a release slice that is thin but still usable end to end
cards.use: need to see the whole journey before choosing what to build first
not: is a flat list sorted only by estimated cost

cards.subject: A spike
says: is a short time-boxed investigation to reduce uncertainty
produces knowledge rather than shippable features
is used when a story cannot be estimated because something is unknown
cards.use: cannot estimate a story until you learn how an unfamiliar API behaves
not: is a story that must deliver working code to users

cards.subject: A use case
says: describes how an actor interacts with a system to reach a goal
has a main success scenario and alternative flows
is more detailed than a typical user story
cards.use: need a step-by-step description of an interaction with its failure paths
not: is a single sentence naming role, action and benefit

cards.subject: An actor
says: is a role outside the system that interacts with it
can be a person or another system
is named by role rather than by an individual's name
cards.use: need to name who or what starts or takes part in an interaction
not: is a step inside the system's internal processing

cards.subject: A stakeholder
says: is anyone affected by or able to influence the system
may never use the system directly
includes sponsors, regulators and support staff as well as users
cards.use: need to find all the people whose needs must be considered
not: is only a person who logs in to the system

cards.subject: The main success scenario
says: is the sequence of steps when everything goes right
is also called the basic flow or happy path
has numbered steps alternating between actor and system
cards.use: describe the normal route to the goal
not: lists what happens when the user is not allowed

cards.subject: An alternative flow
says: describes a valid variation or failure branch from the main steps
refers to the main step where it branches
captures unhappy paths such as invalid input
cards.use: need to record what happens when a service is down
not: is the only path a use case may contain

cards.subject: A precondition
says: states what must be true before a use case can begin
is checked or guaranteed by something outside the use case steps
examples include that the user is signed in
cards.use: need to say the user must already be authenticated
not: states what is true after the use case ends

cards.subject: A postcondition
says: states what is true after the use case completes
describes the observable state change such as a saved record
can differ between success and failure endings
cards.use: need to say what the system looks like at the end
not: states what must hold before the first step

cards.subject: A use case diagram
says: shows actors and the goals they pursue with the system
uses ellipses for use cases and stick figures for actors
gives an overview but not the detailed steps
cards.use: need a one-page picture of who does what with the system
not: shows the order of messages between objects over time

cards.subject: A sequence diagram
says: shows messages between participants in time order
is drawn with lifelines running down the page
belongs to design more than to early requirements
cards.use: need to show the order of calls between services
not: lists all actors and goals on one page

cards.subject: An activity diagram
says: shows a workflow as actions, decisions and parallel branches
reads like a flowchart with swim lanes for roles
helps expose gaps in a business process
cards.use: want to model a process with decision points and handoffs between teams
not: shows only the static structure of data

cards.subject: An entity relationship diagram
says: shows the data entities and how they relate
helps check that the requirements cover all the data to be stored
records cardinality such as one to many
cards.use: need to agree the data a system must hold
not: shows who may perform which actions

cards.subject: Performance
says: measures speed such as response time and throughput
is stated against a defined load
is verified by a load or stress test
cards.use: need a page to respond within an agreed time for most requests
not: is the length of time the service is allowed to be down

cards.subject: Availability
says: is the share of time the service is able to work
is stated as an allowed amount of downtime
is paired with a recovery target after a failure
cards.use: must state how much downtime the business can accept
not: is the number of requests handled per second

cards.subject: Scalability
says: is the ability to handle growing load by adding resources
is expressed as the growth the system must absorb
can be vertical or horizontal
cards.use: expect user numbers to grow tenfold over a year
not: is the ease of fixing a defect in the code

cards.subject: Reliability
says: is the probability the system runs without failure for a period
is described by measures such as mean time between failures
concerns correct operation rather than just being up
cards.use: need the system to complete work correctly over a long run
not: is how quickly the system can be restored after an outage

cards.subject: Security
says: protects data and functions from unauthorised access or change
includes authentication, authorisation and encryption needs
is verified by reviews and testing such as penetration tests
cards.use: must state who can see and change sensitive data
not: lets users with disabilities use the product

cards.subject: Privacy
says: limits how personal data is collected, used and shared
turns legal duties into behaviour such as consent and deletion
is wider than keeping data secret
cards.use: must handle personal data in line with data protection rules
not: is only about preventing hackers from breaking in

cards.subject: Usability
says: measures how easily the intended users reach their goals
is judged with real users on real tasks
is stated as task success rate or time to complete
cards.use: need new users to complete a first task without help
not: is the amount of load the system can carry

cards.subject: Accessibility
says: ensures people with disabilities can use the product
includes support for screen readers and keyboard navigation
is verified by an audit against a recognised standard
cards.use: must allow a screen reader user to complete the same tasks
not: is about how quickly pages load on slow networks

cards.subject: Maintainability
says: is how easily the system can be understood, changed and fixed
is helped by modular design and tests
affects the long-term cost of ownership
cards.use: expect the team to change the product often for years
not: is how many users the system can serve at the same time

cards.subject: Portability
says: is how easily the system can run in a different environment
is reduced by tight coupling to one platform
is stated as a list of platforms that must be supported
cards.use: must run on more than one operating system or cloud
not: is how easily one developer can read another's code

cards.subject: Recovery time objective
says: is the longest time the business accepts to restore service after a failure
is set by the business rather than by the engineers
drives the cost of the backup and failover design
cards.use: need to say how long an outage may last
not: is the maximum amount of recent data that may be lost

cards.subject: Recovery point objective
says: is the maximum period of data loss the business accepts
decides how often backups or replication must run
is measured backwards in time from the failure
cards.use: need to say how much recent data can be lost after a failure
not: is the longest time to bring service back

cards.subject: A role
says: is a named set of permissions
is assigned to people rather than defined per person
reflects a job function such as reviewer or administrator
cards.use: need to give a group of people the same access
not: is the login name of one individual

cards.subject: A permission
says: allows one specific action on one kind of resource
is combined into roles
is checked every time the action is attempted
cards.use: need to decide who may view, edit or approve a thing
not: is a job title in the organisation

cards.subject: The principle of least privilege
says: gives each user only the access needed for their job
reduces the harm from mistakes and stolen accounts
is reviewed again when someone changes job
cards.use: deciding the default access for a new role
not: gives everyone administrator rights to avoid support requests

cards.subject: Separation of duties
says: requires that no one person can complete a sensitive process alone
stops the author of a change from also approving it
limits both error and fraud
cards.use: find that the person who prepares a filing could also close it
not: lets one administrator do every step so work is faster

cards.subject: A permissions matrix
says: lists roles against actions in a table
shows who may view, create, edit, approve or delete
gives a test case for every cell including the denied ones
cards.use: need one place that shows who may do what
not: is a diagram of the system's servers

cards.subject: Role-based access control
says: grants access through roles
makes changes easier because you edit the role not every user
can become messy if there are too many roles
cards.use: want access to follow job functions
not: decides access from attributes such as time and location on each request

cards.subject: Attribute-based access control
says: decides access by evaluating attributes of the user, the resource and the context
can express rules such as only during working hours from a managed device
is more flexible but harder to review than plain roles
cards.use: need rules that depend on context as well as job
not: assigns fixed permissions to named roles only

cards.subject: The joiner, mover, leaver process
says: covers granting, changing and removing access as people's jobs change
includes ending access immediately when someone leaves
prevents access that outlives a job
cards.use: need to prevent leftover access after a person changes team or leaves
not: describes how new features move from design to release

cards.subject: An access review
says: is a periodic check that current access still matches current need
finds orphaned and excessive accounts
is run by the owners of each system or role
cards.use: want to find permissions nobody needs any more
not: is the first sign-in test of a new account

cards.subject: A role-permission denied case
says: is a test that proves a user without the right is refused
checks that the refusal gives no clue about hidden data
is needed as much as the allowed case
cards.use: must test that an unauthorised user cannot reach a record
not: is a test of the main success scenario only

cards.subject: A compliance requirement
says: turns an external rule into specific system behaviour
has a named source such as a law, standard or contract
needs input from the people responsible for legal matters
cards.use: learn the product must follow a data protection law
not: is a preference expressed by one user

cards.subject: A consent requirement
says: asks for a clear agreement before personal data is made public
is recorded so it can be shown later
may be withdrawn by the person
cards.use: need a user to agree before name and photo become visible to others
not: hides all personal data from every other user

cards.subject: A data retention rule
says: sets how long data is kept before deletion
balances legal duty to keep against duty to delete
is implemented as a scheduled and tested purge
cards.use: need to delete records after a legally set period
not: records who agreed to a data use

cards.subject: An audit trail
says: records who did what and when
is protected against change by the people it records
supports compliance and investigation of incidents
cards.use: must prove who approved a sensitive action
not: is a backup of the database

cards.subject: Data residency
says: requires that data is stored in a particular country or region
affects the choice of hosting and suppliers
is a constraint that must be known before architecture is chosen
cards.use: learn customer data may not leave a region
not: decides how long data may be kept

cards.subject: An integration requirement
says: states what data flows to or from an external system
names an owner for the credentials and the interface
says what happens when the other system is unavailable
cards.use: must connect to a payment, tax or social platform
not: describes the colour scheme of the user interface

cards.subject: An interface contract
says: defines the format, fields and rules of an exchange between systems
lets both sides build and test independently
must be versioned when it changes
cards.use: need two teams to build against an agreed message format
not: is a legal agreement between a company and a user

cards.subject: A third party limit
says: is a restriction set by an external platform that the product cannot change
must be captured as a requirement early
can decide which features are possible at all
cards.use: find that a platform offers no write interface
not: is a quality target set by your own team

cards.subject: A fallback path
says: defines what the system does when an integration fails
may queue work for later or hand it to a person
is tested by simulating the outage
cards.use: need work to continue when an external service is down
not: is a second copy of the whole system in another region

cards.subject: A privacy impact assessment
says: reviews how a feature handles personal data before it is built
identifies risks and the controls that reduce them
is carried out early enough to change the design
cards.use: plan a feature that collects new kinds of personal data
not: measures how fast the feature responds

cards.subject: Requirements traceability
says: links each requirement to its source, design, test and release
shows which tests cover which requirement
helps assess the impact of a change
cards.use: must show every requirement has been built and tested
not: ranks requirements by value

cards.subject: A traceability matrix
says: is a table linking requirement identifiers to other artefacts
exposes requirements with no test
exposes work items with no requirement behind them
cards.use: want to find gaps in test coverage against requirements
not: lists which role may do which action

cards.subject: Forward traceability
says: follows a requirement on to design, code and tests
shows whether a requirement was implemented and verified
answers where a requirement ended up
cards.use: want to check a requirement was built and tested
not: follows a test back to the need that justified it

cards.subject: Backward traceability
says: follows a work item back to the requirement that justified it
finds gold plating with no source
answers why a thing was built
cards.use: find code or a feature nobody asked for
not: follows a requirement on to its tests

cards.subject: A requirement identifier
says: is a unique stable number given to each requirement
is never reused when the requirement is deleted
lets everyone refer to the same item
cards.use: need to refer to a requirement in tests and release notes
not: is the priority level of a requirement

cards.subject: A baseline
says: is a reviewed and approved version of a set of requirements
is the reference point for later changes
changes only through a formal change process
cards.use: need an agreed version to measure scope change against
not: is the lowest priority group in a ranking

cards.subject: Impact analysis
says: estimates what a proposed change would affect
uses traceability links to find affected design, tests and documents
is done before a change is approved
cards.use: must say what a late change would touch before approving it
not: is a test of the finished product

cards.subject: Requirement status
says: records where a requirement is, such as proposed, approved, built, tested or dropped
makes progress visible across the whole set
is updated as each stage completes
cards.use: want a quick view of how much agreed scope is finished
not: is the importance of a requirement to the business

cards.subject: Requirement attributes
says: are data kept with each requirement such as owner, priority, source and status
make filtering and reporting possible
are chosen to be few enough to keep up to date
cards.use: need to report on requirements by owner and priority
not: are the steps of a use case

cards.subject: MoSCoW
says: ranks items as must, should, could and won't have this time
fixes the must-haves needed for the release to work
makes explicit what is out of scope for now
cards.use: need a simple four-way ranking for a release
not: scores items by reach, impact, confidence and effort

cards.subject: The Kano model
says: classes features as basic, performance or delighter
explains why meeting basic needs gains no extra satisfaction
uses user survey answers to place features
cards.use: want to know which features users merely expect and which excite them
not: ranks items in four groups from must to won't

cards.subject: RICE scoring
says: scores items by reach, impact, confidence and effort
produces a number to compare unlike items
depends on estimates that should be challenged
cards.use: need a consistent score to compare many items
not: groups items into must, should, could and won't

cards.subject: Weighted scoring
says: scores each item against criteria that carry different weights
makes the criteria and their importance explicit
depends on agreeing the weights first
cards.use: need to compare options on cost, risk and value together
not: fixes the number of each priority level

cards.subject: Cost of delay
says: measures the value lost for each period a feature is not available
helps rank items that are urgent but small
is estimated with the business
cards.use: must choose between a quick fix and a larger project that loses value daily
not: is the cost to build the feature

cards.subject: A minimum viable product
says: is the smallest release that lets you test the key assumption
is chosen to learn rather than to be complete
still has to work well for the users it serves
cards.use: want to test whether users value an idea before building all of it
not: is a prototype that is thrown away without users seeing it

cards.subject: Priority inflation
says: happens when too many items are marked as top priority
removes the ability to choose
is countered by a cap on how many must-haves are allowed
cards.use: find that 90 percent of requirements are marked critical
not: is a rise in the cost of the project over time

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: is the uncontrolled growth of scope after it was agreed
happens through many small unreviewed additions
is controlled by a change process
cards.use: see small extra requests slip in without any review
not: is a formal approved change to the baseline

cards.subject: A trade-off decision
says: records which of two conflicting qualities was chosen and why
prevents the same argument being reopened
has a named owner and date
cards.use: find that speed and cost conflict and one has to give
not: lists the rejected features

cards.subject: An ambiguous requirement
says: can be read in more than one way
uses words such as fast, easy or secure with no measure
is fixed by adding a number, a condition or an example
cards.use: find a requirement that says the page must load quickly
not: has an identifier but no owner

cards.subject: An untestable requirement
says: cannot be checked to give a clear pass or fail
lacks a measure or an observable result
is rewritten with a threshold and a method of verification
cards.use: cannot design a test for a requirement as written
not: is a requirement that contradicts another one

cards.subject: A conflicting requirement
says: contradicts another requirement
is found by reviewing requirements against each other
is resolved by the stakeholders with authority
cards.use: find two requirements that cannot both be met
not: has no source or owner

cards.subject: A solution-biased requirement
says: prescribes how to build instead of what is needed
limits design choices without reason
is rewritten to state the underlying need
cards.use: read a requirement that names a specific database for no stated reason
not: states a measurable quality

cards.subject: A compound requirement
says: packs several needs into one statement
is hard to test because parts may pass and others fail
is split so each statement has one condition
cards.use: find a requirement joined by and that bundles three behaviours
not: is a requirement with a numeric threshold

cards.subject: A weak word
says: is a term such as appropriate, user-friendly or etc that hides detail
is searched for during a requirements review
is replaced by a measurable statement
cards.use: scan requirements for terms that can't be checked
not: is a priority label

cards.subject: A measurable criterion
says: states a quantity and a condition under which it is checked
lets two people reach the same verdict
for example, says 90 percent of requests finish within an agreed time under a stated load
cards.use: turn a vague quality into something verifiable
not: describes the feeling the user should have

cards.subject: A requirements review
says: checks requirements for clarity, completeness, consistency and testability
involves users, developers and testers
finds defects at the cheapest point in the project
cards.use: want defects found before design begins
not: tests the finished software with real data

cards.subject: An inspection
says: is a formal review with defined roles and a checklist
records defects found and measures the review's yield
is used where the cost of missed errors is high
cards.use: need a rigorous, measured review of a critical requirements document
not: is an informal chat about the draft

cards.subject: A missing requirement
says: is a need that nobody wrote down
often relates to error handling, security or a rarely used role
is found by checking against use cases and the permissions matrix
cards.use: find that the unhappy paths were never specified
not: is a requirement with two meanings

cards.subject: A change request
says: is a formal proposal to alter an approved requirement
records the reason, the impact and the decision
is assessed before work begins
cards.use: hear a stakeholder ask to add a feature after sign-off
not: is a bug report about released software

cards.subject: A change control board
says: is the group that approves or rejects proposed changes
weighs impact on cost, schedule and risk
keeps a record of decisions
cards.use: need an accountable body to decide on changes
not: is a team that writes the code

cards.subject: Change control
says: is the process that governs how baselined requirements may change
prevents uncontrolled changes
is lighter in agile work but still present
cards.use: need a clear route for altering agreed scope
not: is the testing of software changes

cards.subject: Version control for requirements
says: keeps a history of every revision of the requirements
lets you compare and restore earlier versions
shows who changed what and when
cards.use: need to see how a requirement looked three months ago
not: decides which changes are approved

cards.subject: A requirements volatility measure
says: tracks how often requirements change over time
signals unstable scope or poor early analysis
is used to adjust plans and contingency
cards.use: want evidence that scope is moving too much
not: counts the defects found in testing

cards.subject: An emergency change
says: is made quickly outside the normal path because of urgent risk
is still recorded and reviewed afterwards
should be rare and have a clear approver
cards.use: must fix a security flaw today before any board can meet
not: is a change scheduled at the end of each quarter

cards.subject: A backlog refinement session
says: is a regular meeting to clarify, split and re-order upcoming stories
keeps requirements current in agile work
involves product owner and team
cards.use: want stories understood before they enter a sprint
not: approves a change to a signed-off baseline

cards.subject: A product owner
says: decides the order and acceptance of the work for the team
is the single voice of the business for the backlog
accepts or rejects completed stories
cards.use: need one person to decide priorities and answer questions
not: is the person who writes the code for each story

cards.subject: Validation
says: checks that the requirements describe what stakeholders actually need
asks are we building the right thing
is done with users and business owners
cards.use: want to be sure the requirements are the right ones
not: checks that the software matches the specification

cards.subject: Verification
says: checks that the product meets its stated requirements
asks are we building it right
is done by tests, inspections and analysis
cards.use: need to show the build matches the specification
not: checks that the requirements reflect real user needs

cards.subject: A prototype
says: is an early model of the system used to get feedback
lets users react to something concrete
may be thrown away or evolved
cards.use: users cannot say what they want until they see it
not: is the final signed-off document

cards.subject: A wireframe
says: is a simple outline of screen layout with no styling
is cheap to change
focuses on structure and flow rather than appearance
cards.use: want to agree a screen's content and layout quickly
not: is a working version of the code

cards.subject: User acceptance testing
says: is testing by the business users to confirm the system fits their needs
uses real scenarios against the acceptance criteria
is the last gate before release in many projects
cards.use: need users to confirm the finished system before go-live
not: is testing by the developers of their own code

cards.subject: A walkthrough
says: is a session where the author steps through the requirements for feedback
is less formal than an inspection
reveals misunderstandings early
cards.use: want a quick informal review with stakeholders
not: is a formal review with a defect log and checklist

cards.subject: A pilot
says: is a limited real-world release to a small group
tests the requirements in live conditions
lowers the risk of a full launch
cards.use: want evidence from real use before a full rollout
not: is a paper review of a draft

cards.subject: An A/B test
says: compares two versions with different users at the same time
uses real behaviour to judge which meets a goal better
needs a clear metric chosen first
cards.use: cannot agree which of two designs will work better
not: is a review by the project sponsor

cards.subject: A requirements elicitation interview
says: is a one-to-one conversation to learn a stakeholder's needs
uses open questions
is followed by a written summary for confirmation
cards.use: want to learn needs in depth from a single expert
not: is a written survey sent to many people

cards.subject: A requirements workshop
says: brings stakeholders together to agree needs
surfaces conflicts in the room
is led by a facilitator
cards.use: need to resolve differing views quickly in one session
not: is a one-to-one conversation with a single user

cards.subject: A requirements document
says: records the agreed requirements in one place
has a unique identifier for each requirement
is reviewed and signed off by named stakeholders
cards.use: need a shared reference for what will be built
not: is a record of test results

cards.subject: A product backlog
says: is an ordered list of everything that may be built
is kept current by the product owner
replaces a large up-front specification in agile work
cards.use: work iteratively with changing priorities
not: is a baselined document that never changes

cards.subject: A glossary
says: defines the terms used in the requirements
stops different people using one word for different things
is shared by business and technical staff
cards.use: find that two teams mean different things by customer
not: lists the people who signed off the document

cards.subject: The scope statement
says: states what is included and what is excluded
protects against assumptions about extra features
is part of the signed baseline
cards.use: must settle what is out of scope
not: lists every use case step

cards.subject: Stakeholder sign-off
says: is formal approval that the requirements are accepted
is given by people with authority to decide
makes later changes subject to change control
cards.use: need agreement before design and build start
not: proves the requirements are correct and complete

cards.subject: A sign-off authority matrix
says: lists who may approve which kind of requirement
avoids sign-off by someone with no authority
is agreed before the review starts
cards.use: find that nobody knows who can approve a regulatory item
not: lists which user roles may use the system

cards.subject: A software requirements specification
says: is a formal document of functional and non-functional requirements
is aimed at designers, developers and testers
follows a structure such as a recognised standard
cards.use: need a complete formal statement of what the system must do
not: is a plan of the project's tasks and dates

cards.subject: A context diagram
says: shows the system as one box with the external actors and systems around it
fixes the boundary of the system
lists the data flowing across the boundary
cards.use: need to show what lies inside and outside the system
not: shows each step of a use case in order

cards.subject: The limits of sign-off
says: gives the team an agreed reference but does not make the content right
does not remove the need to validate with users
can lock in errors if change control is too rigid
cards.use: hear that sign-off means the requirements cannot be wrong
not: makes any later change impossible

cards.subject: The gglearn level exam rule
says: draws 10 questions for a level exam
needs 80 percent to pass
unlocks the next level once a learner passes
cards.use: want an example of a functional rule that can be tested directly
not: lets a learner skip any level at will

cards.subject: The gglearn open answer grading
says: grades open answers against a reference answer and a rubric
uses a coarser keyword fallback when there is no API key
is a functional requirement with a stated fallback
cards.use: want an example of a requirement that names its fallback
not: is graded by a person only

cards.subject: The gglearn production Node version
says: runs on Node 20 in production
means code must avoid newer APIs
needs a native SQLite package version with a prebuilt binary for that Node
cards.use: want an example of a constraint that comes from the platform
not: is a feature chosen by the learners

cards.subject: The gglearn private contest rule
says: returns a 404 to outsiders
hides the existence of the contest
is a privacy requirement written as behaviour
cards.use: want an example of privacy turned into a testable rule
not: shows the contest to anyone with the link

cards.subject: The gglearn public contest rule
says: needs a consent box before joining
makes name, photo and progress public
can go from public to private but never back
cards.use: want an example of consent and an irreversible state change
not: can be made public again by an administrator after going private

cards.subject: The gglearn photo upload rule
says: limits uploaded photos by size and type
rejects SVG files
is a security requirement as well as a usability one
cards.use: want an example of an input restriction requirement
not: accepts any file type up to a size limit

cards.subject: The gglearn offboarding requirement
says: ends a leaver's access immediately
is handled by administrators
is part of the joiner, mover, leaver lifecycle
cards.use: want an example of a leaver requirement
not: keeps access for a notice period by default

cards.subject: The ggsocial approver role
says: can sign off a post
cannot edit the post
makes the approver different from the person who changed the text
cards.use: want an example of separation of duties in content approval
not: can edit and publish any post alone

cards.subject: The ggmoney second person approval
says: requires a second person to approve a filing
refuses self-approval
stops the person who did the work from closing it
cards.use: want an example of a four-eyes control on a filing
not: lets the preparer close the filing after a review of their own work

cards.subject: The ggsocial platform publishing limit
says: lets only 45 of 109 platforms publish automatically
routes 64 platforms with no write API to a manual queue
shows how platform limits shape the product
cards.use: want an example of a third party limit written as a requirement
not: lets all 109 platforms publish automatically

cards.subject: The ggmoney HMRC dependency
says: depends on HMRC submission
needs the company's own credentials
is an integration that must be planned for ownership of credentials
cards.use: want an example of an integration whose credentials the company holds
not: uses credentials supplied by each customer's accountant

qa.q: What does a functional requirement describe?
qa.right: What the system must do
wrong: How fast the system must respond
qa.why: Functional requirements state behaviours or functions.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-functional requirement?
qa.right: The service must be available 99.9 percent of each month
wrong: A user can reset their password by email
An administrator can add a new reviewer
A learner can retake an exam
qa.why: Availability is a quality of the system, not a function.

qa.q: What does a user story usually contain?
qa.right: A role, an action and a benefit
qa.why: The common form is as a role, I want an action, so that a benefit.

qa.q: What is the purpose of acceptance criteria?
qa.right: To decide objectively whether a story is done
qa.why: Criteria are checks that give a pass or fail verdict.

qa.q: Who is a stakeholder?
qa.right: Anyone affected by or able to influence the system
qa.why: Stakeholders include indirect parties such as regulators.

qa.q: Why is the word fast a poor word in a requirement?
qa.right: It cannot be measured or tested
qa.why: No threshold means no pass or fail test.

qa.q: What is the main aim of traceability?
qa.right: To link each requirement to its source, design and tests
qa.why: Traceability shows coverage and impact.

qa.q: A requirement says the system must be user-friendly. What is the best first improvement?
qa.right: State a measurable target, such as the share of new users who finish a task without help
wrong: Ask the developers to decide what it means
qa.why: A measurable criterion makes it testable.

qa.q: What is the difference between validation and verification?
qa.right: Validation checks we are building the right thing; verification checks we built it right
wrong: Validation is done only by developers
Verification is done only by users
qa.why: Validation relates to the need; verification relates to the specification.

qa.q: Which MoSCoW category holds items that are explicitly out of scope for this release?
qa.right: Won't have this time
qa.why: The W records what is deliberately deferred.

qa.q: What is a baseline?
qa.right: An approved version of the requirements that changes only through change control
qa.why: Baselines give a fixed reference for later changes.

qa.q: Which technique lets users react to something concrete before it is built?
qa.right: Building a prototype
qa.why: Prototypes make needs visible.

qa.q: What does the Given-When-Then format express?
qa.right: A starting state, an action and an expected result
qa.why: It comes from behaviour-driven development.

qa.q: A permissions matrix is useful because it
qa.right: shows who may view, create, edit, approve or delete, giving a test for each cell
qa.why: Each cell, including denied ones, becomes a test.

qa.q: Why should each requirement have a unique identifier?
qa.right: So tests, designs and release notes can refer to the same item
qa.why: Stable identifiers support traceability.

qa.q: Which of these is an actor in a use case?
qa.right: An external payment system that sends a confirmation
wrong: A line of the main scenario
qa.why: Actors are outside the system, and can be systems.

qa.q: Which quality attribute is measured by task success and time to complete for real users?
qa.right: Usability
qa.why: Usability is judged with users on tasks.

qa.q: A team writes: The system shall be secure and easy to use and respond quickly. What is wrong?
qa.right: It bundles several vague needs into one untestable statement
qa.why: It is both compound and ambiguous.

qa.q: A story is too big to finish in a sprint. What should the team do first?
qa.right: Split it into smaller stories that still deliver value
wrong: Start it and finish next sprint
Lower its priority to won't have
qa.why: Splitting keeps work small and testable.

qa.q: A stakeholder asks for a new feature after sign-off. What should the analyst do?
qa.right: Raise a change request and assess its impact before deciding
wrong: Add it quietly to the baseline
Ask the developers to start at once
qa.why: Changes to a baseline go through change control.

qa.q: Which statement shows separation of duties?
qa.right: The person who approves a post is not the person who changed its text
wrong: One administrator can do every step of a process
All users share a single account
qa.why: No one person can complete a sensitive process alone.

qa.q: Why include unhappy paths in requirements?
qa.right: Failure, invalid input and denied access are where many defects occur
qa.why: Alternative flows capture what happens when things go wrong.

qa.q: What does the INVEST checklist test?
qa.right: Whether a story is ready: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable
qa.why: It is a quality check on stories.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.right: Precondition: true before the use case starts; postcondition: true when it ends
wrong: Precondition: true after it ends; postcondition: true before it starts
qa.why: Preconditions come first, postconditions after.

qa.q: What does backward traceability help you find?
qa.right: A feature that has no requirement behind it
qa.why: It follows work back to its source.

qa.q: A requirements review is most valuable
qa.right: before design begins, because defects are cheapest to fix then
wrong: only at the end of testing
only when the budget is cut
qa.why: Early defects cost less.

qa.q: What is the best way to document a constraint such as an older production runtime?
qa.right: Record it in the requirements with an owner and how it will be verified
wrong: Leave it to the deployment team
Add it to the glossary only
qa.why: Constraints belong in the requirements so nobody discovers them late.

qa.q: What is the difference between the definition of done and acceptance criteria?
qa.right: The definition of done applies to all stories; acceptance criteria are specific to one story
wrong: Acceptance criteria apply to all stories
The definition of done is for stakeholders only
qa.why: One is a shared quality bar and the other is per story.

qa.q: A requirement says the system must use a particular database product with no reason given. What kind of defect is this?
qa.right: Solution bias: it prescribes how rather than what
qa.why: The underlying need should be stated instead.

qa.q: A learner needs 80 percent on a 10 question exam. Which acceptance criterion is correct?
qa.right: Given 10 answered questions, when 8 are correct, then the exam is passed and the next level unlocks
qa.why: It is specific and testable with numbers.

qa.q: You find two requirements that contradict each other. What should you do?
qa.right: Take both to the stakeholders with authority and record the decision
qa.why: Conflicts are resolved by those who own the decision.

qa.q: A requirement says 90 percent of searches finish within two seconds under 500 users. How should it be verified?
qa.right: With a load test at the stated load
wrong: By asking users if it feels fast
qa.why: Measurable criteria need a matching verification method.

qa.q: A platform offers no write interface. What is the right requirement response?
qa.right: Capture the limit and specify a manual fallback such as a queue
wrong: Assume it will be added later
qa.why: Third party limits shape what can be promised.

qa.q: The business can tolerate one hour of outage but only five minutes of lost data. Which statement is correct?
qa.right: The recovery time objective is one hour and the recovery point objective is five minutes
wrong: The recovery time objective is five minutes and the recovery point objective is one hour
qa.why: RTO is time to restore; RPO is data loss window.

qa.q: A leaver still has access a month after leaving. Which requirement was missing?
qa.right: A joiner, mover, leaver process that ends access immediately
qa.why: Access that outlives a job is a common risk.

qa.q: Users keep changing their minds when they see the finished work. What practice would have helped most?
qa.right: Early prototypes and regular validation with users
qa.why: Validation earlier exposes mismatched needs.

qa.q: A traceability matrix shows requirement 12 with no test. What does this mean?
qa.right: There is a gap in verification that must be closed
qa.why: Untested requirements are unverified.

qa.q: Which is the best use of a spike?
qa.right: To investigate an unknown so a story can be estimated
wrong: To deliver a feature to users
qa.why: Spikes buy knowledge.

qa.q: The privacy rule says a private contest must not reveal that it exists. How should the system respond to an outsider asking for it?
qa.right: Return a not found response, as if it did not exist
wrong: Redirect to the sign in page
qa.why: A 404 does not confirm existence.

qa.q: A requirement states the system must handle growth. Which rewrite is best?
qa.right: The system must support 10,000 concurrent users with response times unchanged
qa.why: A numeric target is testable.

qa.q: Everyone marks their requirements as must have. What is the best response?
qa.right: Introduce a cap or a forced ranking and discuss trade-offs
qa.why: Priority inflation removes choice.

qa.q: A signed-off document is found to contain a wrong requirement. What does this show?
qa.right: Sign-off gives an agreed reference but does not guarantee correctness
qa.why: Validation still matters after sign-off.

qa.q: Which question best finds missing requirements?
qa.right: What happens when this fails, and who else needs access?
wrong: How many pages does it have?
qa.why: Failures and minor roles are the common gaps.

qa.q: Which statement about attribute-based access control is true?
qa.right: It evaluates attributes of user, resource and context, so is more flexible but harder to review
wrong: It is just a list of roles
It forbids rules based on time
qa.why: It trades simplicity for flexibility.

qa.q: A security flaw must be fixed today. How should change control handle it?
qa.right: Allow an emergency change with a named approver and review it afterwards
wrong: Wait for the next board meeting
qa.why: Emergency paths are controlled, not absent.

qa.q: Speed and cost conflict. What should the analyst do?
qa.right: Record a trade-off decision with owner and rationale
qa.why: Documented decisions stop the argument reopening.

qa.q: A new feature collects a new type of personal data. When should a privacy impact assessment be done?
qa.right: Before design is fixed, so findings can change it
qa.why: Early review can change the design.

qa.q: You can't estimate a story because an external API is unfamiliar. What is best?
qa.right: Run a time-boxed spike and report what you learn
wrong: Wait for the vendor to explain
qa.why: Spikes reduce uncertainty.

qa.q: Why is a non-functional requirement costly to add late?
qa.right: It shapes the architecture, so changing it can mean redesign
wrong: It affects only the user interface
qa.why: Qualities cut across the whole system.

qa.q: Which is a good reason to use a story map?
qa.right: To see the whole user journey and slice a thin usable release
qa.why: It arranges stories along the journey.

qa.q: A context diagram shows
qa.right: the system as one box with the external actors and data flows around it
qa.why: It fixes the system boundary.

qa.q: A business rule says refunds above a set amount need manager approval. How should it appear in the requirements?
qa.right: As a numbered rule with the threshold, the approver role and a test for the denied case
wrong: As a note in the meeting minutes
As a general statement that approvals are needed
As part of the glossary only
qa.why: A rule needs precise terms to be testable.

qa.q: Why is Given-When-Then useful to testers?
qa.right: Each scenario can be turned directly into a test
qa.why: The format is close to executable examples.
